title: Big churches and house churches
hookLine: Christians gather in stadiums and in living rooms

cards: Three thousand. Then, two or three. Both numbers are in the New Testament, and both describe a church.
On a Sunday you can find each shape. An arena: a full parking lot, a band on a stage, lyrics on screens the size of houses, a crowd you can't see the end of.
And a living room: a sagging couch, two kitchen chairs, a pot of soup on the stove for after. Someone reads a psalm. Someone else admits a hard week.
The people in both rooms would call it church.

teach.h: ABOUT THREE THOUSAND IN A DAY.
teach.b: Big or small? The question goes back to the church's earliest pages, and the Bible doesn't pick a side.
In Acts, on the day of Pentecost, Peter preaches to a crowd in Jerusalem, and in the King James Bible: "the same day there were added unto them about three thousand souls."

teach.h: IN THE TEMPLE, AND FROM HOUSE TO HOUSE.
teach.b: A few lines later, here's how those same people lived: "continuing daily with one accord in the temple, and breaking bread from house to house, did eat their meat with gladness and singleness of heart."
The temple courts and the kitchen table, both, daily. Paul's letters send greetings to churches that meet in people's homes: "Likewise greet the church that is in their house."
The Greek word behind church, ekklesia, means an assembly, a gathering. It fits a crowd, and it fits a couch. Today the two shapes live side by side.
Big churches can put on worship that lifts a whole arena, run food banks, and give a newcomer a seat where nobody notices them yet.

House churches can know every name, notice who's missing, and carry each other's groceries. Each has its critics and its defenders, and some big churches split into small home groups during the week to get both.

teach.h: WHERE TWO OR THREE ARE GATHERED.
teach.b: Under it all sits a promise Jesus made in Matthew about the smallest gathering of all: "For where two or three are gathered together in my name, there am I in the midst of them."
Read that way, God doesn't wait for a crowd.

how: Christians gather in congregations of every size, from large churches with several services each weekend to small groups meeting in homes, and some large churches organize their members into weekly home groups for prayer and Bible study.

games.why: "continuing daily with one accord in the temple, and breaking bread from house to house." from the start, the church was both big and small.

practice: If someone is with you, do this together; if not, bring to mind two or three people you'd want in that living room, not the impressive ones, the ones you'd let see a hard week.
Notice who came to mind first, and who you're surprised to miss. If you pray, pray for each of them by name; if not, hold them one at a time with good will.

wordCard.voice: Ekklesia. The New Testament word for church, an assembly that fits a crowd of thousands or a gathering in someone's house.
